paras: The killing of Crockett Jenkins was the hanging of a man described as a member of the Campbell gang, whose body was found on a hilltop oak near Princeton in Caldwell County, Kentucky, in late September 1882. One Kentucky paper called it another hanging by a mob, but the fuller accounts said suspicion fell on Mary Sullivan and female relatives, who were arrested and released. The case drew attention chiefly because Mary Sullivan was herself hanged by a mob from the same limb about a week later.

Papers described the Campbell gang, sometimes called the Campbell-Sullivan gang, as a band of Caldwell County 'outlaws, murderers and robbers', and Jenkins as 'another notorious member'. According to the Louisville Commercial, Jenkins had lived with Mary Sullivan for about two years, but some weeks before his death he turned to another woman, and she was said to have threatened to kill him and to have attacked him in a quarrel. Shortly before, a mob had attacked the Campbells, killing members of the family, an event the papers treat as a separate hanging.

The Louisville Commercial reported that some men returning from a neighbor's at night thought they heard a man pleading for mercy with someone they believed was called 'Mary'. The next day Jenkins's body was found hanging from the limb of a large oak at the top of a hill, a few miles from Shady Grove according to the Crittenden Press. A Louisville dispatch dated October 5 put the discovery about two weeks earlier, and the Hartford Herald reported the death by September 27.

Two Sullivan women were arrested and taken to Princeton; the Louisville dispatch named them as Mary and Jane Sullivan and said they were tried and released. The Madisonville Times said they were freed 'through lack of any evidence', while the Louisville Commercial, which named Mary, her mother and her sister, said there was 'no positive proof' against them.

On the night of September 29, a mob took Mary Sullivan from Norman Hubbard's house in Hopkins County and hanged her from the same tree and limb. The Madisonville Times said it was unknown whether her killers were the Regulators who had hanged the Campbells or friends of the gang avenging Jenkins. No report of an inquest or of any other charge in Jenkins's death appears in the coverage.

Coverage came entirely from white papers, and Jenkins's death was rarely reported on its own. The Louisville dispatch folded it into a string of Caldwell County hangings and ran in eastern papers under 'Lynch Law in Kentucky' and, in Martinsburg, 'Wholesale Lynching in Kentucky', which said the gang was being 'rapidly decimated by the outraged people'. The Louisville Commercial's long narrative, reprinted from Washington and St. Paul to Arizona, treated Jenkins as a character in a story of Mary Sullivan's 'lawless love and lawless hate'.

Kentucky papers took varied lines: the Crittenden Press called his death 'disgraceful', while the Hartford Herald, condemning a later mob hanging of a woman, cited Mary Sullivan's 'complicity in the recent murder of Crockett Jenkins' as some excuse for her own lynching.

Accounts differ over who killed Jenkins: the Hartford Herald's first notice called it a hanging by a mob, while the Louisville dispatch, the Madisonville Times and the Louisville Commercial pointed to the Sullivan women. The Madisonville Times added that Jenkins had 'whipped and maltreated' the two women the day before he died, but none of the papers names a witness, and the women were released.

reader.title: Killing of Crockett Jenkins
bases: Jenkins was found hanged and the Hartford Herald called it a hanging by a mob (A6), but the Louisville dispatch, the Madisonville Times and the Louisville Commercial attribute the killing by accusation to Mary Sullivan and one or two female relatives after a personal quarrel (A8, A13, A20), so neither a mob killing nor a private homicide is established.

Jenkins was hanged without legal authority (A6, A8, A20), but only the Hartford Herald's one-line notice calls it a mob hanging (A6), while the fuller accounts name as suspects two or three Sullivan women said to be acting from jealousy or after a whipping, a personal motive rather than a claim of justice (A13, A16, A20); the killers were never identified.

That Jenkins was found hanged in Caldwell County is reported independently by the Hartford Herald, the Louisville dispatch, the Madisonville Times, the Crittenden Press and the Louisville Commercial (A6, A8, A11, A13, A20), but who hanged him is disputed between 'a mob' (A6) and the Sullivan women (A8, A13, A20).

framing.detail: The Hartford Herald noted the death as Caldwell County's 'another hanging by a mob' and later, while condemning mob law over a woman's hanging, treated Mary Sullivan's 'complicity in the recent murder of Crockett Jenkins' as established.
